entries: From Middle High German valden, valten, from Old High German faldan, faltan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan. The irregular forms with -t- arose through early levelling of Grammatischer Wechsel, but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. They probably established themselves in modern German by analogy as there are several verbs in -alten (halten, schalten, spalten, walten), but none in -alden.

entries: Of dialectal origin, particularly German Low German nee (“no”). Cognate to Dutch nee, English no.

Likely originally a pronunciation spelling of 'n, 'ne, representing final devoicing, then generalized to other forms of the article. Possibly influenced by mmh and the spelling of English nasal interjections such as hngh.
Possibly also motivated by a dispreference for single-letter words, which are not typical for German orthography (compare also the similarly proscribed merging of 'n into 'nen).
senses: a, an (any indefinite article, regardless of the case or gender of its referent)
